title: Finding Freedom Through Ethical Conduct - Liberty
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the difference between freedom and liberty, defining liberty as the responsible use of freedom without depriving anyone else, and cites Abraham Lincoln's line that the right to swing a fist ends where another person's nose begins. Kanho quotes Ibram X. Kendi's Stamped from the Beginning on racial discrimination and asks listeners to keep learning where their own liberty ends. Two Buddhist supports follow: the paramitas, and the precepts as read from the San Francisco Zen Center full moon ceremony, which Kanho frames as voluntary limits on freedom. The story of Siddhartha's four sights and great renunciation leads to Mary Oliver's poem on the Buddha's last instruction, "Make yourself a light."

Sorry for the brief delay; my chisha needed to get me some water because I was really feeling dry.
I have been fortunate enough to receive the COVID vaccine some days ago, and unfortunately, it did make me quite sick, so I'm not 100% yet.
Thank you for your patience and thank you for being here on such a beautiful day.

This morning, I was thinking that once the weather gets better, our attendance will probably drop because people will be so wanting to go outside into the sunshine, and I realized that's quite all right; that's actually perfect.
Let's enjoy the sun and summer, good weather while it lasts.
Also, it really means so much to me that you're here and I can see you on my screen, even though you're only this big.
So thank you very much.
It's not quite as good as wrapping elbows in the zendul, but we'll refrain from that for a little bit longer.
Still, it gives me a very warm feeling to see you all here.
Today, I am going to keep my talk relatively short, I hope, so we can engage in a longer conversation together in the end.
All our voices are important in times like these.
I also regret to inform you that this talk, like so many others, simply did not want to conform to the ideas I had originally; even the title needed correction.

So I thought today I was going to talk about finding freedom through ethical conduct, and that worked out all right until I looked at definitions and I went into the word liberty, which seems to describe much better what I was looking for.
I still think the first version sounds a lot better, so yes, I needed to use the word liberty.
I'm going to torture you by taking you along for my brief detour through definition land.
Liberty can be differentiated from freedom.

The word freedom seems to mean primarily the ability to do whatever one wants to do, and what one has the power to do, so freedom seems to be more broad in that it represents a total lack of restraint.
One definition said unrestrained ability to fulfill one's desires.
When we use the word liberty, we mean the absence of arbitrary restraints, and we are taking into account the rights, not only of oneself, but also of all the others involved.
In this sense, the exercise of liberty is subject to capability and limited by the rights of others.
I stole this verbatim from one of the dictionaries: *Liberty entails the responsible use of freedom without depriving anyone else of their freedom*.

Here is an extreme example: a person can have the freedom to shoot someone, to kill someone, but they do not have the liberty to do it because that deprives the other person of their right not to be harmed.
It deprives the other person of their freedom.
The French novelist Victor Hugo addressed it by saying, *the liberty of one citizen ends where the liberty of another person begins*.
I like this one.
In truly American fashion, President Abraham Lincoln explained that *my right to swing my fist ends where your nose begins*.
So now we are forced to reconcile with the notion of freedom, and this reckoning is coming in these days; we're going through right now.
We are living in times where ideas of freedom and liberty clash.
Over the last decade, we have watched as words have been used and abused until we no longer recognize them.
We have seen power used and abused to the point where the original idea has been lost.
We have seen our political representatives absorbed in striving for personal power and personal gain until we no longer recognize the office they were to embody.
You have seen a black man die while in police custody, and now we are all experiencing the ongoing criminal lawsuit; there is no escape.
We want to believe in a way that all this is new and we can fix it right now, but it is not new.
I am now quoting from the most excellent book, stamped from the beginning by Ibrahim X.
Kendi.
So this is the quote: *I was taught the popular folk tale of racism that ignorant and hateful people had produced racist ideas, and that these racist people had instituted racist policies.

But when I learned the motives behind the production of many of America's most influentially racist ideas, it became quite obvious that this folk tale, though sensible, was not based on a firm footing of historical evidence.
Ignorance, hate, racist ideas, discrimination.
This causal relationship is largely ahistorical.
It has actually been the inverse relationship.
Racial discrimination led to racist ideas, which led to ignorance and hate.
Racial discrimination, racist ideas, ignorance, hate.
This is the causal relationship driving America's history of race relations.*
End quote.

Here is another powerful quote from the same book: *When you truly believe that the racial groups are equal, then you must also believe that racial disparities must be the result of racial discrimination.* You may feel a bit uncomfortable at this point; you came to hear a Dharma talk related to awakening and practice realization, something maybe that will help you with your meditation, but this really does have to do with awakening.
For me to awaken, to realize liberty, I must understand how my freedoms impact everybody else.
Yes, in spite of COVID-19, it is absolutely fine, and I have the freedom to not wear a mask, but not when other people are around.
My freedom to do whatever I want is limited by the right of others to remain free from disease and healthy.
Why did I quote Ibram Exkendi?
Because he taught me much, much that I had not known, and he taught me to think in new ways about what I am observing.
He revealed to me prejudiced ways I was thinking.

Let me repeat that quote from before: *When you truly believe that the racial groups are equal, then you also believe that racial disparities must be the result of racial discrimination.* So I let you figure out what that means for you.
I have this request: please keep on learning, looking, and seeing deeply, expanding our understanding of where our liberties end and to understand where the liberty of our fellow beings begin.
I am asking that we pay attention, remain fluid, don't build walls around our privilege.
I am asking us not to freeze into inaction either, because that's quite a possibility.
It starts in our own home.
We learn that the particles of our favorite microfiber clothing ends up in the ocean.
Our car exhaust accelerates global warming.
Climate refugees.
Borders.
Child immigrants.
Melting glaciers.
The appearance that we are in the middle of the sixth great extinction.
I could go on for quite a while, so let's do what we can.
Let's not get frozen by the magnitude of what surrounds us, but let's not ignore it.
Let's not remain passive.
Let's keep sitting with it and feeling into it.
Let us learn where our liberty ends and someone else's nose begins.
So our Buddhist practice offers us two paths, well, many more, but I will limit myself to two today that might support this personal endeavor.
And so I would like to speak just a little bit about the paramitas and the precepts.
I think most of us are familiar with both.
We studied the paramitas last summer, and so if you go to our website, you might actually find a series of talks about them.
There are also some excellent books among them: *The World Could Be Otherwise* by Norman Fischer and *The Six Perfections* by Dale Wright.
So the paramitas, the shortest of cliff notes, brief tour: in Mahayana Buddhism, in Zen, we propagate the bodhisattva ideal with the paramitas as one of the core values.

In short, the paramitas are the perfection of generosity, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor or energy, the perfection of concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Did I forget the perfection of concentration?
The parameters are part of the bodhisattva ideal, and let's imagine that we all are bodhisattvas striving for this.
We are striving for our desire to awaken, so we can arouse this desire, we can hold on to it, and we can expand this desire to awaken for the benefit of all beings.
This is part of the Mahayana path, and it is one of the healthy desires, the ones that benefit us and everybody else.
The original ideal of awakening was to awaken, to cross the finish line into nirvana, never to be reborn again.
For us, it's a little bit different.
Our goal is primarily to reborn infinite numbers of times so we can liberate all beings still trapped in this cycle of birth and death.
So this was really the Cliff Notes version of the paramitas.
And the other path is the precepts.
And so we can maybe look at the precepts with new eyes, or listen with new ears might be better.
I have chosen a different version of them; I'm going to read the San Francisco Zen Center full moon ceremony.
*I'll skip the first part, and I'll start with the refuges that we chanted also today: I take refuge in Buddha before all being, immersing body and mind deeply in the way, awakening true mind.
I take refuge in Dharma before all being, entering deeply the merciful ocean of Buddha's way.
I take refuge in Sangha before all being, bringing harmony to everyone free from hindrance.
Now the pure precepts: I bow to refrain from all evil.
This is the abode of the law of all Buddhas.
It is the source of the law of all Buddhas.
I bow to make every effort to live in enlightenment.
It is the teaching of Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi, and the path of the one who practices and that which is practiced.
I vow to live and be lived for the benefit of all beings.
It is transcending, profane and holy, and taking self and others across.
Now the grave precepts: I vow not to kill.
By not killing life, the Buddha tree seed grows.
Transmit the life of Buddha and do not kill.
I bow not to take what is not given.
The self and objects are such as they are.
Two, yet one.
The gate of liberation stands open.
I bow not to misuse sexuality.
Let the three wheels of self, object and action be pure.
With nothing to desire, one goes along together with the Buddhas.
I bow to refrain from false speech.
The Dharma wheel turns from the beginning.
There is neither surplus nor lack.
The sweet dew saturates all and harvests the truth.
I bow to refrain from intoxicants.
Originally pure, don't defile.
This is the great awareness.
I bow not to slander.
In the Buddha Dharma, go together, appreciate together, realize together and actualize together.
Don't permit false finding.
Don't permit haphazard talk.
Do not corrupt the way.
I bow not to praise self at the expense of others.
Buddhas and ancestors realize the vast sky and great earth.
When they manifest the noble body, there is neither inside nor outside in emptiness.
When they manifest the Dharma body, there is not even a bit of earth on the ground.
I bow not to be avaricious.
One phrase, one verse.
That is the 10,000 things and 100 grasses.
One Dharma, one realization.
It's all Buddhas and ancestors.
Therefore, from the beginning, there has been no stinginess at all.
I bow not to harbor ill will.
Not negative, not positive.
Neither real nor unreal.
There is an ocean of illuminated clouds and an ocean of bright clouds.
I bow not to disparage the three treasures.
To expound the Dharma was this body is foremost.
The virtue returns to the ocean of reality.
It is unfathomable.
We just accept it with respect and gratitude.*
So by willing to follow the precepts, we are voluntarily limiting ourselves.
We renounce some of our freedoms.
In our practice, renunciation is the act of rejecting something, especially if it is something that the renunciant has previously possessed, practiced, enjoyed, or endorsed.
In religion, renunciation often indicates an abandonment of pursuit of material comforts in the interest of achieving enlightenment.
I'm almost at the end of my talk, but I would like to tell you a short story first.
It is a story of the great renunciation.
At the birth of Prince Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha-to-be, priests predicted that he would either become a great teacher or a world ruler.
However, the prince's father had specific ideas; he wanted to have his son follow in his footsteps.
So the prince was not allowed to see anything unpleasant or harmful.
He was really coddled, lived a life of luxury.
But during his childhood, young Prince Siddhartha had a strong meditation experience while he was sitting under a tree watching the laborers in the fields.
But I think he must have forgotten about it in a way, because it was not until he was in his late twenties that he had the urge to go beyond his comforts.
And together with his charioteer, Channa, he went to explore.
He saw four things in there, known as the four sights, actually.
He saw an old person.
Siddhartha had never seen an old person before, so he asked his charioteer what he was looking at.
Channa said, yeah, everybody gets old, and then they look like this.
And when Siddhartha saw an ill person, he was upset because he'd never seen anything like that before.
But Channa explained, yeah, we all get ill sooner or later.
The third sight was a dead person, and Channa explained to his prince that everybody will die.
The fourth sight was a holy man, a monk, and this person made Siddhartha really curious because the monk was so calm and serene in the middle of all the hustle and bustle and suffering.
So Siddhartha chose his own path.
He left family, wife, son, palace, servants, wealth, and became an ascetic.

The archaeologist Alfred Fouche, 1865 till 1962, pointed out the significance of the great renunciation: it's the point that all of a sudden Siddhartha was no longer a prince and he could no longer ask the deities for assistance.

And as such, he found himself in an indifferent world without guidance or support, confronted with both the noble task of seeking mankind's salvation and the lowly but pressing one of securing his daily bread.
End quote, Fouche.
We know that the Buddha to be studied.
We know that he almost starved himself to death, and we know that he awakened when his flawless eyes saw the morning star.
He said, *Through the many rounds of my birth, I roamed without reward, without rest, seeking the house builder.
Painful is birth again and again.
House builder, you are seen.
You will not build a house again.
Your rafters broken, the rich pole destroyed, gone to the unformed.
The mind has come to the end of craving.*
Now we are really almost at the end of the talk, but I thought I would leave you with something beautiful.
I will end with Mary Oliver's poem.
I've read it here before and I'll probably read it again.
And it's Mary Oliver's, *The Buddha's last instruction: Make yourself a light, said the Buddha before he died*.
I think of this every morning as the East begins to tear off its many clouds of darkness to send up the first signal, a white fan strict with pink and violet, even green.
An old man, he laid down between two sala trees, and he might have said anything, knowing it was his final hour.
*The light burns upward, it thickens and settles over the fields.
Around him, the villagers gathered and stretched forward to listen.
Even before the sun itself hangs, disattached in the blue air, I am touched everywhere by its ocean of yellow waves.
No doubt he thought of everything that had happened in his difficult life.
And then I feel the sun itself as it blazes over the hills, like a million flowers on fire.
Clearly I am not needed, yet I feel myself turning into something of inexplicable value.
Slowly, beneath the branches, he raised his head.
He looked into the faces of that frightened crowd.* Thank you very much for listening to this little bit different Dharma talk.
And if you could gather something from it, that's great.
And if not, please utterly forget it and just return to your practice.
May our intention equally extend to every being in place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
